newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to play role in Swiss Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to play role in Swiss Holocaust fund.

text.p: The major participants in the battle over Switzerland's handling of wartime Jewish assets on Friday publicly declared an end to their confrontation as the United States offered its help in setting up a fund for Holocaust victims.

A three-hour meeting between Jewish leaders and Swiss, Israeli and U.S. officials ended with previously warring participants hailing a new spirit of cooperation to resolve what has been called the last chapter of the Holocaust -- a battle over how to compensate victims.

"Things are back on track after getting out of hand and emotional," World Jewish Congress President Edgar Bronfman said, at a news conference in which he was flanked by the chief U.S. and Swiss officials dealing with the issue.
Earlier, Switzerland's chief critic in the U.S. Senate, Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, declared himself satisfied that a new page has been turned in Swiss-Jewish relations.

D'Amato, who for weeks has been accusing Swiss bankers of acting as Hitler's money-launderers, praised the new spirit of cooperation evident at the meeting, made possible by the creation of a fund to help Holocaust victims.

The Swiss government, which six weeks ago said it would never establish such a fund, announced this week that it would take over a private $71 million fund set up by the country's three biggest banks and work with the WJC and Swiss Jews to set up a mechanism for its "timely distribution."
Bronfman said that payments could begin as early as this summer.

Private Swiss businesses and other banks are now making more donations to the fund -- bringing its total to more than $100 million so far. The Swiss government is also planning to make a contribution, although that may, under Swiss law, have to be ratified in a national referendum.

U.S. Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat, who is preparing a major report on Swiss-Nazi relations, pledged that the United States would act as a facilitator in seeing that the fund gets off the ground and is "orderly, organised, transparent and accountable."
Thomas Borer, the chief Swiss negotiator, said his government was "fully committed to righting the wrongs of the past."

Details of how the fund was to be set up and exactly how it would benefit Holocaust survivors were to be decided in meetings between the Swiss government and Jewish groups that were expected to start next week in Berne.

Sources close to the negotiations expected a foundation to be set up to administer payments and give priority to the neediest survivors and those who never received any compensation, like the Jews of Eastern Europe.
Establishment of the fund does not prejudice efforts by individuals to retrieve unclaimed funds deposited in the Holocaust era that may still be in Swiss banks, participants at the meeting said.

Eizenstat said he was encouraging other countries -- especially those in Europe that were neutral -- to set up commissions to examine their relationships with the Nazis and consider making donations to the humanitarian fund.
Sweden, Norway, Portugal and Austria are establishing commissions and France is taking a new look at the actions of the Vichy government.

Eizenstat's report on Swiss-Nazi relations is expected to be released at the end of March. It draws heavily on materials gathered by the United States just after the war when it tracked Nazi assets, including the gold the Germans looted from the countries it conquered.
